headline: Xabi Alonso wins first game as Chelsea boss in 3-2 thriller vs Fulham
summary: Morgan Rogers scores on debut for the Blues, while Joao Pedro finds the net after just 31 seconds of play.
details: Xabi Alonso secured a winning start to his tenure as Chelsea manager, leading the team to a pulsating 3-2 victory over Fulham at Craven Cottage on Monday.
The match began with an explosive start as Joao Pedro scored for Chelsea after just 31 seconds. However, a blunder by keeper Robert Sanchez allowed Fulham's Josh King to equalize in the 23rd minute.
Morgan Rogers, the most expensive British player in history at 117 million, made an immediate impact by scoring on his debut to put Chelsea back in the lead before half-time.
Cole Palmer further extended the advantage after the break, but another mistake by Sanchez gifted Fulham a second goal through Gonzalo Garcia.
The victory marks a strong first impression for Alonso, who was hired to revive a Chelsea side that finished 10th in the Premier League last season.
The match also featured a reunion of old friends, as Alonso faced off against new Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa, with whom he played for years at Real Madrid, Liverpool, and Spain.
caption:
A 117m debut goal and a 31-second strike! Xabi Alonso kicks off his Chelsea era with a 3-2 win.

Cole Palmer further extended the advantage after the break, but another mistake by Sanchez gifted Fulham a second goal through Gonzalo Garcia.

The victory marks a strong first impression for Alonso, who was hired to revive a Chelsea side that finished 10th in the Premier League last season.

The match also featured a reunion of old friends, as Alonso faced off against new Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa, with whom he played for years at Real Madrid, Liverpool, and Spain.

headline_marked: US universities urge [[international students to return by Sept 15]]
headline: US universities urge international students to return by Sept 15
summary: Top institutions like Harvard and Columbia warn that new federal immigration rules will change how stay durations are calculated for F-1 and J-1 visa holders.
details: Top US universities, including Harvard, Columbia, and the University of Chicago, are urging international students to return to the US before September 15 to avoid complications from new federal immigration rules.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is replacing the long-standing 'Duration of Status' (D/S) system with a fixed-term stay system for F, J, and I category visa holders.

Under the new rules, students entering or re-entering the US after September 15 will receive a specific end date on their Form I-94, typically based on their course duration with a maximum initial term of four years.
This change significantly impacts students in long-term programs, such as doctoral or medical degrees, who may now need to apply for extensions through USCIS if their studies exceed four years.
Students already present in the US on September 15 and maintaining their status will generally fall under interim rules and won't need to apply for new stay approvals immediately.
Because of this, universities like Columbia have requested students return as early as September 8, while others emphasize that returning before the 15th avoids the new fixed-term restrictions.
The University of Chicago has organized emergency webinars to explain the stricter restrictions and the shortened 30-day grace period associated with the new policy.
The new policy has already been challenged in federal court by several higher education organizations and labor unions.

This change significantly impacts students in long-term programs, such as doctoral or medical degrees, who may now need to apply for extensions through USCIS if their studies exceed four years.

Students already present in the US on September 15 and maintaining their status will generally fall under interim rules and won't need to apply for new stay approvals immediately.

Because of this, universities like Columbia have requested students return as early as September 8, while others emphasize that returning before the 15th avoids the new fixed-term restrictions.
